title: Nibble and Marmalade's Woodland Bake-Off
markdown:
Young Leo, master of a thousand toy kingdoms, lay asleep. In the basket, two small hearts declined to join him.

Nibble the hamster, who treated hours as if they could be stacked, squeaked, “The hour is nigh, Marmalade.”

Marmalade the bunny, fluff expanding with each thought, blinked. “Nigh for what? Has Leo left a moon-carrot?”

Nibble sighed, which in a hamster is a serious wind. “The Woodland Whispers Baking Contest. Judged by Luna herself. The moon.”

“Ooh. Baking.” Marmalade’s ears unfurled. “Carrots? A giant cake of clover?”

They slipped from the basket. Nibble consulted a dried leaf of plans. Mission one: ingredients. Flour, honey, three plump blueberries, tied into a handkerchief with the satisfaction of a knot that meant business.

“To the woods. Speed and stealth.”

On the dewy lawn a soft mist began, the sort that makes fur look decorated whether you asked or not.

“A minor inconvenience,” Nibble muttered.

Marmalade leapt. “The heavens weep for our baking. A sign!” He twirled. Each spin announced them to every listening blade of grass.

“Marmalade. Please. This is pastry.”

The woods received them like old guards who had seen worse. The path climbed. A wooden bridge over a brook took the moonlight and gave it back in pieces. Marmalade stopped so hard his ears arrived a moment later.

“A ladder of starlight.”

Nibble, who did not hold with poetry during timed events, still nodded. “The gateway.”

The clearing shimmered as if the moon had put on an apron. Tables held acorn biscuits, berry tarts, meringues that looked too proud to sit down. The judges watched: an owl with spectacles on his beak, a squirrel with a tail like a verdict. Serious faces. The kind that have tasted disappointment and kept notes.

Nibble unveiled the dough, a recipe he had perfected in the quiet of his own head — flour, and a notion of captured moonlight that he would not have admitted to a squirrel. “Our prize brioche awaits.”

Marmalade mashed blueberries with a whisper of honey. “Now. The grand finale. A cascade of flavour.”

The flourish was spectacular and wrong. Most of the berries missed the brioche and found the moss. A sad puddle clung to the crust, like a thought that had arrived too late and too wet.

Nibble stared. Plans, which he had believed were a kind of armour, went thin. “Marmalade. A disaster. Damp. Sprawling.”

Marmalade’s ears dropped. He looked at the smeared brioche, then at the judges’ puzzled tilt. “I was trying to make it grand.”

Rain ticked on leaves. Nibble’s whiskers sagged. The secret journey, the leaf of plans, the knot in the handkerchief — all of it seemed to have been a rehearsal for this particular splat.

Then something small and stubborn lit. “No. Not undone. Re-imagined.” He considered the puddle as if it had applied for a job. “Not a cascade. A glaze. Rustic. Honest. Forest-floor.”

He nudged Marmalade. “You have a talent for honest enthusiasm. We tell them. The simple truth.”

They presented. Nibble’s voice did not shake, which surprised him. “Esteemed judges. Our brioche was meant to be a spectacle. An enthusiastic incident with the drizzle has resulted in this.”

Marmalade, clear as a bell that had decided not to pretence: “I got very, very excited. The drizzle travelled further than planned. Nibble says it’s a rustic glaze now. That’s important.”

The owl peered, eyes magnified into fairness. The squirrel leaned in, sniffed, tasted. Silence did the difficult work.

“Hmm,” hooted the owl. “The brioche is light. Airy. Perfectly baked. And the glaze—” a twinkle, not quite a joke — “unexpectedly vibrant. The forest floor after rain.”

The squirrel’s tail flicked. “It speaks of honesty. Resilience. You faced an unexpected turn and did not falter. Culinary spirit.”

So Nibble the planner and Marmalade the bouncy dreamer were crowned champions of the Woodland Whispers, not for a cascade, but for a puddle they had refused to disown. They scampered home as the drizzle stopped. The moon, who may or may not have been judging, laid silver on the path as if that, too, were a kind of glaze, and they carried the handkerchief back empty, which is how you know a contest has been properly eaten.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
